q: In the figure, which group shows a parallel force system?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: In group B every line of action points the same way (vertical), so the forces are parallel. Gravity loads on a beam form a parallel system. Group A is concurrent and group C is neither.

q: What is the SI base unit of mass?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Mass is one of the seven SI base quantities and its unit is the kilogram. The newton is a derived unit for force, so a mass of 1 kg weighs about 9.81 N on Earth.

q: What is a scalar quantity?
o: A quantity with magnitude and direction, such as force
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time or temperature
A quantity that is always negative
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: A scalar is fully described by a number and a unit. Force, velocity and displacement need a direction as well, so they are vectors.

q: What is the resultant of a force system?
o: The largest force in the system
The force needed to hold the system in equilibrium
The sum of the magnitudes, ignoring direction
The single force that has the same net effect as the whole system
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: The resultant replaces all the forces with one that pushes the body the same way. The force that would balance them is the equilibrant, equal in size and opposite in direction. Adding magnitudes without direction is wrong for vectors.

q: What is the SI unit of force?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: The newton is a derived unit: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². The pascal is force per area (N/m²) and the joule is work (N·m).

q: A load spread over an area, such as a floor live load, is expressed in which unit?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Area loads are force per unit area, kN/m², which is the same as kPa. NSCP live loads, for example 1.9 kPa for residential floors, are given this way. Line loads are in kN/m and point loads in kN.

q: What is the weight of a 50 kg mass, using g = 9.81 m/s²?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: W = mg = 50 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 490.5 N, or about 0.49 kN.

q: Which relation gives the weight of a body?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Weight is the gravitational force on a mass: W = mg. It is Newton's second law (F = ma) with the acceleration set to g.

q: In the figure, which beam carries a uniformly distributed load?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Beam B has the same load intensity all along its length, shown as a rectangle of equal arrows. For analysis it can be replaced by one resultant w × L acting at midspan. A carries a point load and C a triangular load.

q: Which branch of mechanics studies bodies in motion and the forces that accelerate them?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Dynamics covers bodies that accelerate. It has two parts: kinematics (the motion itself) and kinetics (the forces behind it). Statics covers bodies at rest or moving at constant velocity.

q: Which three things fully describe a force?
o: Magnitude, direction and point of application
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: A force is a vector, so it needs a size and a direction. On a rigid body its line of action (point of application) also matters, because moving a force sideways changes the moment it causes.

q: What are coplanar forces?
o: Forces that all pass through one point
Forces that are all equal in size
Forces that act at different times
Forces whose lines of action all lie in the same plane
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Coplanar forces lie in one plane, so they can be drawn in 2D and solved with three equations (ΣFx, ΣFy, ΣM). Most beam and truss problems are planar.

q: What is the SI base unit of length?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: The metre is the SI base unit. Millimetres and kilometres are the same unit with prefixes, and the foot belongs to the English system.

q: In the figure, which beam carries a concentrated (point) load?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Beam A has one load acting at a single point, drawn as one arrow and expressed in kN. A column resting on a beam or a heavy machine is usually idealized this way.

q: A force of 100 kN acts at 30° above the horizontal. What is its horizontal component?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Fx = F cos θ = 100 × cos 30° = 100 × 0.866 = 86.6 kN. The vertical component is F sin θ = 50 kN.
steps: F = 100 kN, θ = 30° from the horizontal

q: How is one newton defined?
o: The weight of a 1 kg mass at the surface of the Earth
The force needed to lift a 1 kg mass through a height of 1 m
The pressure a 1 kg mass exerts when resting on 1 m²
The force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s²
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: From F = ma, 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s². The weight of 1 kg on Earth is about 9.81 N, not 1 N. Lifting 1 kg by 1 m is work (about 9.81 J).

q: Which of these is a body force, acting on every particle of a body rather than on its surface?
o: A column bearing on a footing
Soil pressure on a retaining wall
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Body forces act through the whole volume, like gravity (self-weight) and the inertia forces of an earthquake. Wind pressure, bearing and soil pressure are surface forces applied at contact.

q: Which field deals with the effects of forces on bodies, and includes statics and dynamics?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Engineering mechanics applies physics to engineering problems. Its two main parts are statics (bodies at rest) and dynamics (bodies in motion). Strength of materials builds on it.

q: What value of standard gravity, g, is normally used in structural calculations?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Standard gravity is 9.80665 m/s², rounded to 9.81 m/s². The value 32.2 is the same acceleration in ft/s².

q: In the figure, which beam carries a load whose intensity changes along its length?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Beam C carries a triangular (uniformly varying) load, such as soil or water pressure that grows with depth. Its resultant equals the area of the triangle, ½wL, acting at one-third of the span from the heavy end.

q: What conditions must a planar rigid body satisfy to be in equilibrium?
o: The largest force must equal the smallest
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: In equilibrium the body neither moves nor rotates, so the net force in both directions and the net moment about any point must all be zero. These three equations are the basis of statics.

q: What is a vector quantity?
o: A quantity with both magnitude and direction
A quantity that only applies to motion
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Vectors, such as force, displacement, velocity and acceleration, must be added head to tail or by components, not simply by adding numbers.

q: In the figure, which group shows a concurrent force system?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: In group A all the lines of action meet at one point. A concurrent system has no moment about that point, so only ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 are needed, as at a truss joint.

q: What is the SI base unit of time?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: The second is the SI base unit of time. Minutes and hours are accepted for use but are not SI base units, and the hertz (1/s) measures frequency.

q: A load spread along the length of a beam, such as a wall on a beam, is expressed in which unit?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: A line load is force per unit length, kN/m. A 3 m high wall weighing 2.5 kPa, for example, puts 7.5 kN/m on the beam under it.

q: What is a reaction in structural mechanics?
o: The load applied to a floor by its occupants and furniture
A force or moment that a support develops in response to the loads
The weight of the member itself, acting at its center of gravity
The deflection of the member measured at the point of load
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Supports push back on the structure. The reactions are found from equilibrium (in a determinate structure) and then become the loads on whatever lies below, such as columns and footings.

q: Which equation is Newton's second law of motion?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Force equals mass times acceleration. mv is momentum and ½mv² is kinetic energy.

q: A 20 kN load acts 3 m from point O, perpendicular to the lever arm. What moment does it cause about O?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: M = F × d = 20 kN × 3 m = 60 kN·m. The unit is kN·m, force times distance, not kN/m.

q: Which branch of mechanics studies bodies at rest or moving at constant velocity?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: Statics deals with bodies in equilibrium, where the acceleration is zero. Buildings are designed mostly with statics. Dynamics (with its parts, kinematics and kinetics) handles accelerating bodies.

q: In the figure, which group shows a non-concurrent, non-parallel force system?
ref: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Statics; Beer & Johnston, Vector Mechanics for Engineers
n: In group C the lines of action neither meet at one point nor run parallel. Such a system can cause both translation and rotation, so all three equilibrium equations are needed.
